recap.back_html: Racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic, biometric (to identify), health, sex life, sexual orientation.
Yes. A model that infers health or ethnicity processes special category data.
recap.front_html: Is an inferred special category special category data?

recap.back_html: Protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010. Not special categories.
An Article 6 lawful basis for all personal data, plus an Article 9 condition for special category data.

lessons.takeaway_html: Classify each attribute by what it reveals. Keep the special categories and the protected characteristics as two separate fields, and treat inferences as data.
lessons.title: Personal data, special category data and the two-part test

recap.back_html: Consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests, and recognised legitimate interests since 5 February 2026.
Rarely appropriate. The power imbalance makes it hard to give freely. Use another basis.
Purpose, necessity, balancing, recorded before processing starts.
A basis covers the purposes you specified. A new purpose, such as an attrition model, needs its own check.
Article 6(1)(ea), from 5 February 2026. Only the purposes in Annex 1, with no balancing test.

lessons.takeaway_html: Give each purpose its own lawful basis, avoid consent for workers, record a legitimate interests assessment for each use of legitimate interests, and keep only the fields each purpose needs.
lessons.title: A lawful basis for each use of talent data

recap.back_html: Article 9(2)(b) plus Schedule 1, Part 1, paragraph 1 of the DPA 2018, with an appropriate policy document.
Article 9(2)(g) plus Schedule 1 paragraph 8, equality of opportunity or treatment. Never for decisions about one person.
Names the Schedule 1 condition, how you meet the principles, and retention and erasure. One APD can cover several purposes.
Before high-risk processing, always for large-scale special category data and extensive profiling with significant effects. Consult the ICO if high risk remains.

lessons.takeaway_html: Pair each Article 9 condition with its Schedule 1 condition and an appropriate policy document, keep monitoring data away from individual decisions, and screen every new use for a DPIA.
lessons.title: Article 9 conditions, policy documents and DPIA screening in HR

recap.back_html: Description and purposes, necessity and proportionality, risks to people, and the measures that address them.
recap.front_html: Article 35(7): four required parts of a DPIA

recap.back_html: Likelihood: remote, possible, probable. Severity: minimal, significant, severe. Overall: low, medium, high.
In the risk section, with flag rates per group, the ratio and the threshold for action.
recap.front_html: Where fairness goes in a DPIA

recap.back_html: Consult the ICO before processing starts.

lessons.takeaway_html: Cover the four parts of Article 35(7). Name each harm, rate it, put fairness figures in the risk section, record measures and residual risk, and consult the ICO if a high risk remains.
lessons.title: Writing the DPIA for a people model

recap.back_html: Data no longer attributable to a person without additional information that is kept separately and protected.
Yes. You hold the key. It lowers the risk; the law still applies.
A plain hash of a known-format ID is matched by hashing every possible value. HMAC with a secret key prevents that.
Bronze raw for a named few, silver pseudonymised, gold aggregated with small groups suppressed.

lessons.takeaway_html: Keep raw identifiers in bronze for a few people, pseudonymise with a keyed hash in silver, suppress small groups in gold, and record each choice. Pseudonymised data is still personal data.
lessons.title: Personal data in each medallion layer

summary: Personal and special category data, lawful bases for talent data, Article 9 conditions, appropriate policy documents and DPIA screening.
